lessons.title: Is AI actually worth it here?
lessons.subtitle: Net time instead of gut feeling

concept.body:
Two controlled experiments, two opposite results:

| Study | Task | With AI |
|---|---|---|
| Noy and Zhang 2023, 453 professionals | professional writing tasks, e.g. a press release | 40% faster, quality 18% higher |
| METR 2025, 16 experienced developers | tasks in their own large codebases | 19% slower |

Before the METR study the developers expected a 24% speed-up, and afterwards they still estimated it at 20%. **Feeling and measurement were far apart.**

The difference lies in the task: how long do review and rework take? So you measure before you decide. Net time is drafting plus review plus rework, compared with the same task without AI.
concept.takeaway: Measure net time: drafting, review and rework against the same task without AI.

exercise.title: Run the numbers on one of your tasks
exercise.instructions: Set the sliders to a task from your week and meet the three goals. You are done once all three have been reached.

outputs.label: Review and rework as share of AI time

verdicts.title: Slower with AI
verdicts.body: Review and rework eat the gain. Keep the task yourself or shrink it until review is quick.

verdicts.title: Hardly any gain
verdicts.body: Below 20% saving a fixed workflow rarely pays. A template may be enough.

verdicts.title: Net gain
verdicts.body: Confirm the number with a week of real measurement before you fix the workflow.

goals.label: Set a review time at which AI is slower net.
goals.insight: That is how the METR study ended: review and correction cost more than the draft saved.

goals.label: Find a setting with at least 40% saving per run.
goals.insight: That matches the effect in Noy and Zhang. Typical for texts you can check quickly.

goals.label: Bring the rework share down to 10% or less.
goals.insight: Less rework pays off on every run. A better brief or a template earns its keep here.

props.note: Your numbers, your assumptions. Time it for a week before you decide.

checks.prompt: A team feels much faster with AI. What is the next step?

options.text: Roll the workflow out to everyone.
options.feedback: A feeling is not a measurement. In the METR study participants estimated a 20% gain and were 19% slower.

options.text: Time the work with and without AI for a week, including review and rework.
Ask the team how satisfied they are.
options.feedback: Satisfaction matters, but it says nothing about time. For that you need the clock.

checks.explanation: You measure net time by adding drafting, review and rework and comparing the sum with the baseline.

checks.prompt: Why can both studies be right although their results are opposite?

options.text: One of the two studies must have miscalculated.
options.feedback: Both are controlled experiments. The difference lies in the task and the review effort.

options.text: The tasks differ: short writing tasks are quick to check, changes in a large codebase are not.

options.feedback: The METR study used the tools current at the time. What mattered was how much review and correction the task needed.

checks.explanation: The benefit depends on the task. So you measure per task, not across the board.

concept.body:
Dell'Acqua et al. (2023) gave 758 consultants realistic tasks. Inside the model's capabilities they completed 12.2% more tasks with AI, 25.1% faster and at more than 40% higher quality. On a task just outside, they were 19 percentage points less likely to be correct with AI. The frontier is jagged: from the outside you cannot see which side a task is on.

Three questions sort your candidates:

- **Frequency:** how often does the task come up? Rare work does not justify a workflow.
- **Error cost:** what happens if an error slips through?
- **Checkability:** can you spot an error at a glance?

Frequent, cheap when wrong and quick to check: that is where you start.
concept.takeaway: Start where errors are cheap and show up quickly.

exercise.title: Rate eight tasks and add your own
exercise.instructions: Rate every task on the three axes, and add up to three of your own if you like. Evaluate shows the ranking, the matrix and the reference with reasons.

items.text: Standard reply to a frequent customer question
items.why: Daily, an error is quickly corrected, and you see at a glance whether the reply fits.
Weekly. An invented decision or a wrong deadline causes damage, and you have to check against your notes.

items.text: Liability clause in a customer contract
items.why: Rare, expensive when wrong and only checkable with expertise. Not a workflow candidate.

items.text: Translate an internal email into German
items.why: Weekly, internal, and you read the result yourself.
Monthly, and wrong figures feed decisions. Every number needs a check against the source.

items.text: Assign incoming tickets to a category
items.why: Daily and checkable at a glance. A wrong category delays the reply, so the error cost is noticeable.
Errors hit people and stay invisible, because you never see the rejected ones again. Such uses also fall under special rules, see the EU AI Act course.

items.text: Weekly report from the ticket list
items.why: Weekly and internal, but you have to reconcile the numbers with the list.

props.note: The formula is deliberately simple. It does not replace measuring; it only decides what you measure first.

checks.prompt: What does the study with 758 consultants show about the frontier of AI capabilities?

options.text: AI helps evenly with all knowledge tasks.
options.feedback: Outside the frontier participants were 19 percentage points less likely to be correct with AI.

options.text: It is jagged: tasks that look similar can lie on different sides.

options.feedback: The study found gains inside the frontier and losses outside it. The task matters, not only the person.

checks.explanation: Because the frontier is invisible from outside, you start with tasks whose errors you spot quickly.

checks.prompt: Which task belongs at the top of your list?

options.text: The monthly management pack, because it takes the most time.
options.feedback: Rare and expensive when wrong: an error weighs heavily and you learn little.

options.text: Liability clauses, because they are demanding.
options.feedback: Demanding means hard to check and expensive when wrong. That is exactly where you automate last.

options.text: Daily standard replies you can check at a glance.

checks.explanation: Frequent, cheap when wrong, quick to check: there you learn fastest and risk least.
